# Top 5 posts from r/MovieSuggestions day

## 1. What's a movie you love, but you never recommend to anyone?

**Score:** 85
**Body:** You ever finish a movie and think, "I love this.. but I'm not telling anyone to watch it? Maybe it's too weird, too personal, too slow, or just hard to explain without sounding weird.

Whatever the reason, it's your gem, but you keep it quiet. What's that movie for you? I wanna watch it. 


For me, it's not even about being embarrassed. It's more like... know how I connected with it. but I don't guarantee anyone else will. Maybe the pacing's off, the vibe is super niche, or it just hit me at a weird time in life. 


### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Secretary...because it's uh...personally revealing. 
  - We listen & we don't judge
2. Seven Brides for Seven Brothers. I'm ashamed that my number one movie of all time glorifies kidnapping and Stockholm Syndrome, but alas, it is. I'm not afraid to tell people it is my favorite movie of all time, but I hardly ever recommend it, unless someone is looking for a specific type of musical. 
3. I recommend everything but whenever I recommend Waitress (with Kerri Russel), people seem surprised that it’s also a movie.

They turned it into a musical on broadway btw.
4. The Florida Project. It’s brilliant but devastating.
5. I really loved American Beauty when it came out. I still have a soft spot for it. I don’t tell people that now.
6. Time bandits...the original.
7. The Fisher King. I love it. But I've learned recommending it or saying I love it makes people look at me weird after they watch it. 
8. Amelie, I can never quite put into words how this film affects me ( pure instant delight) and so want to share that feeling with others but they don’t seem to ‘get it’. It is my all time favourite film but when anyone asks, they’ve never seen or heard of it so I rarely offer it up.
9. Park Chan Wook's Thirst

## 2. 🎃 Help Me Build My 31 Nights of Halloween Movies! 👻

**Score:** 40
**Body:** Every year I pick 31 movies for October and write them on pieces of paper. Then I draw one from a hat to watch every night. 

Halloween is also my birthday, so I LOVE horror, Halloween, spooky/fall movies, etc.

Unfortunately, work has absolutely kicked my ass this year and I don’t have time to put my list together. 😂

So I’m outsourcing it to Reddit:

*The 31 most-upvoted movie suggestions will become my 31 movies this year.*

No real rules—if it feels like an October movie, throw it in. Horror, Halloween classics, slashers, supernatural, creepy, funny, fall vibes, whatever.

Give me your favorites, hidden gems, or something you think I absolutely NEED to see.

Let’s see if Reddit can build me a hell of a 31-night lineup. Voting/submissions will end on September 30th!

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Something wicked this way comes (1983) 
2. I like the classic horror movies but to kick off fall for me, Its The Great Pumpkin Charlie Brown.
3. "Trick ’r Treat" (2007) - Horror comedy anthology film, that ties up loose ends.
4. Demon Knight (1995) - because I'm always trying to get people to watch it but I think the name or the Tales From the Crypt connection turns them off. 
5. It might be a slightly obvious one, but Halloween (1978) would be a pretty good pick. I think Halloween arguably kicked off the slasher genre of horror. 

Any of the X of the Dead movies directed by George A Romero, specifically either Day of the Dead or Dawn of the Dead. I don’t really consider any of the X of the Dead movies made after George A Romero’s death to be X of the Dead movies. They’re not to be confused with Shaun of the Dead, just to clarify.
6. Arsenic and Old Lace is an absolute Halloween delight!
7. American Werewolf in London  
Edit: Typo on the phone.
8. I'll just say Devil (2010). It's short, only like 80 minutes long, really does a good job at the one small thing it's doing.
9. Ernest scared stupid
10. Does The Devil's Advocate count? 

Barring that, Bram Stoker's Dracula is some campy fun and Keanu being out of place makes it somehow more fun, for me. Delightful miscasting.

I came across Sholay 1975 and dug it, watched it a few more times and realized its a masterpiece on so many levels cinematically. I saw Gangs of Wassepyur Part 1 and loved it. Started watching Pyaasa and loved it (haven't finished it yet). I wanna see all of the great Masala films but they're easily available!

# Top 5 posts from r/moviecritic day

## 1. I want more Sharlto Copley movies!

Excellent actor

I see what you did there.
2. You could do the A-Team movie
  - “You spin me right round baby right round.”

Is probably one of my all time favorite “crazy person thing” done in a movie. 

Like the dude is brilliant, but absolutely nuts and having a blast.

## 2. What is the movie with the most soul-crushing ending?

**Score:** 510
**Body:** For me, the most soul-crushing ending belongs to "***Pan's Labyrinth"***. What a movie, what direction, what everything!  Ofelia leaves this world, and even at the end, we still don't know if she went to the magical eternity she was dreaming of or simply died like everyone else.  Either outcome is extremely painful to bear. It shatters me every time I remember.

### Top 10 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. Melancholia got me. Just dead inside. Mystic River is a gut punch too.
2. Dear Zachary
3. The Mist
4. Grave of the Fireflies - desperately sad. Beautiful, but I never want to watch it again.
5. Kids. Everyone ends up with HIV by the end, which, at the time, was basically a death sentence.
6. Oldboy, the original of course. 
7. Requiem for a Dream. Every character ends the film with their bodies and minds broken by addiction. It is almost guaranteed that none of them will ever recover.
8. Manchester by the sea. Absolutely devastating
9. SE7EN for me. Just kind of sat there for a while…
10. Million Dollar Baby.

## 4. Nolan and Villeneuve both released their first movies in 1998. Thoughts on their careers and futures?

**Score:** 468
**Body:** Denis has firmly cemented himself as **the** sci-fi guy. I really love the set design and visuals of his movies, and the sense of scale that he can evoke. I seriously can’t get enough of his sci-fi aesthetic, like I’ve been unsuccessfully trying to scratch that itch with other movies ever since watching Arrival/BR2049/Dune. With that said it will be nice to see him return to a more grounded world with Bond 26. After that: Rama, Cleopatra, Nuclear War?

Nolan at this point has to be the greatest of this generation, and arguably all time, so I don’t have much else to say. Watching The Odyssey made me realize how much I *needed* fantasy/mythological and horror movies from him. This man has earned the clout to do whatever he wants next, and I can’t wait to see what that will be 👀

### Top 6 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I can confidently and with great certainty predict that both of them will be dead within the span of 100 years.
2. I'm more of a Villeneuve guy personally, but I'll still check out anything these 2 directors do out of curiosity


  - Villenueves movies just have more "sauce" about them. It's hard to explain but both are different and great in their own ways but Nolan is a lot more clinical and Villeneuves movies are just better to look at for the most part
  - people often make the “it’s mainstream” argument but i’m personally happy that at least when i go pay $53 to see a movie in theatres that between these 2 it might be decent. 
3. They're both excellent and have very different styles. Nolan likes bombastic big epic things and Villenueve likes tense up close and personal things. Plenty of room for both and I'm still keen to watch more.
  - Enemy and prisoners were released  on the same year! 

Damn, that must've been busy for him
    - I always find it crazy when a director does two biggish movies in the same year. Like Spielberg with Jurassic Park and Schindler's List... 
4. 2000 - 2014 Nolan

2015 - YTD Villeneuve
  - Crazy good take. Both directors had literally legendary films in the years you mentioned. I have high hopes for Dune III
5. Nolan movies started strong, experiencing a shaky arc qualitywise with his movies themselves (when looked at from a distance in your list), while also rocketing upward at the box office.

Longterm, he needs a strongwilled producer and writer to collaborate with rather than leading everything himself. Particularly writingwise.

Villeneuve career I think has been more of a continuously steady climb so far. Honestly unpredictable.

## 5. What do you think of All Quiet on the Western Front (2022)? How does it rate on its own merits and as an adaptation?

**Score:** 295
**Body:** While many critics initially gave the movie glowing reviews, I think it has a far less positive standing at this point, especially with fans of the original book and 1930 film. In general, it seems to carry a reputation these days of being 'oscar bait'. 

I just rewatched it the other day and am curious what people have to say about it here as there was a pretty wide range of opinions from critics and audiences on the adaptation. 

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. I havnt read the book or saw the original. I loved it personally, although I thought the first half was stronger than the second half. The cinematography and the dread building up in the first 20 minutes blew me away. I really think there's this loop that happened where it just became a fun topic to discuss it as a bad movie, and that gave a % of movie fans who are on the internet a reason to get to skip this watch. I think they want a reason to skip it cus it's a long movie in a foreign language, and it's more fun to say "well actually it sucks.." and that affects the perception of it.
  - yeah that's probably true. that sounds like the way online movie forum people are, anyway. 

your comment reminded me of the beginning which I agree is excellent. I love the commentary on and portrayal of the wartime jingoism/youth indoctrination. it lends the initial warfare scenes a greater sense of impact by putting us in Paul's perspective when everything he has been told is challenged the second he gets to the front line.
    - Of for sure agreed. The sequences in the school, and when picking up his uniforms, are low key incredible. It's easier to point out visually exciting scenes in 1917 and Dunkirk (which are great) but this movie had some amazing shots that really build it up like you said. 

Reddit movie discussion is like.. a fcking nightmare lol. Alot of teenagers finding their identity, and intellectual-complex adults, perpetually gatekeeping, but only watching the same 50 movies. Alright I'll stop venting.
      - reddit fucking sucks but is paradoxically the only place to discuss this kind of thing at all nowadays if you actually want to have people to talk to. 
2. I thought it was a cracking remake. Does make you realise how many young men were killed during that war though. 
3. To me, the whole movie throws the book into the trash, I cannot see it as an adaptation. Maybe it is still the immense disapointement that I felt after seeing it but I also have reasons : 

Firstly, the choice to have the whole story take place in the last weeks or days of the war betrays the intent of the book. The book starts in 1915 or early 1916 (there is a scene where they receive the new steel helmets to replace their leather ones), Paul and the others having enthousiasticly enlisted at the very start of the war. In the movie, we are shown that enthousiasm, but it is absolutely not realistic for 1918 german teenagers (or any other country either) because they would have known what they were going to after four years of war.

The book is a story about resignation, slowly loosing itself in the violence and horror of war and how it makes men become beasts. Some of the most important scenes happen away from the frontline : Paul's leave, the moments where they speak about what they'll do after the war, the visits to their wounded friend. With all that, we see Paul slowly loosing himself over the years, each one of his friends dying taking a piece of his soul. The movie, with it's compressed timeline looses this and the deaths of Paul's friends seems meaningless.

The scenes with the german general are plainly bad, it is very stereotipicaly "german army bad" and the attack on the last day of the war is also in this vein, it happened yes, but the german army was already disintegrating and most of these attacks were led by french and british officers trying to impress their commanders one last time. And it adds nothing to the story.

The scenes with the chancelor are ABSOLUTE BULLSHIT. The fact that they included that in this way is a fucking disgrace and a VERY slippery slope. They showed us some negociations that looked like the chancelor was presented with the Versailles Treaty, and, with the inclusion of some lines like "this will start another war", lends itself to some interpretations not far from the "backstab theory". It is a very dangerous way of rewriting things and should not at all have been included as it doesn't even add anything to the movie except shock factor.

And making the movie end on the eleventh of november 1918, right at the moment of the armistice is just so dumb. Paul dies on a random day of october 1918, his death and that of others so meaningless that on that day, the daily report of the army says "all quiet on the western front". HOW IS THERE NOTHING NEW ON THE WESTERN FRONT ON THE DAY OF THE CEASE FIRE?? They managed to fumble that, *they managed to miss the point of the title of the book!*

So the movie to me, other that the title and some scenes, is not an adaptation of the book, it missed the point and I was hugely disapointed because I really hoped they would make it work. The movie in itself is not bad. Some scenes, the general and the chancelor, are weirdly problematic, others are absurd, like the one where french Saint-Chamond tanks and flamethrowers stop 10meters from a trench, completely out in the open on a strangely flat ground. The general violence and feeling was on point, sound design too.
  - Also makes the whole reason for the fall of the German Kaiserreich nonexistent: a big part was sailor and soldier strikes. These lead to peace discussions and the end of monarchy…
4. As a standalone WWI movie it was alright, but as an adaptation of AQOTWF it was bloody awful, completely missed the mark. I was so disappointed in this movie, it could have been something really great.
5. I love it as a war movie, I agree that it is a bad AQotWF adaption, bc of several issues – not the least of which is the ending.

The whole snobby General and his last push storyline, however, is fucking stupid and ridiculous.
6. Personally, I don't think it is as bad as many make it out to be despite the real faults. It is a very good looking movie in regards to stuff like color grading and cinematography, and is decent at getting themes across (if not hamfisted at times). That being said, it does falter in comparison to the source material.

The movie is probably at its most controversial with the change made to the ending where it replaced the subtle and thematically consistent description of Paul's death with a fictional final bayonet charge. While far inferior as an ending, it does at least still get the point of the film across and probably could have been a lot worse.

At the very least, the movie didn't change to include any jingoism or justification for the conflict like many war movie adaptations end up doing. Also, I could take or leave the new inclusion of armistice negotiations. I do think it makes sense to include something like that in a longer blockbuster adaptation but the scenes' execution was somewhat flawed.

# Top 5 posts from r/TrueFilm day

## 1. Do movies feel less like somebody actually made them now, or am I just getting old?

**Score:** 90
**Body:** There’s a thing I keep trying to put my finger on... A lot of movies now are incredibly well made. Beautiful images. Great actors. Perfect sound. Everybody knows exactly where the story beats go. And yet... They feel like they were designed by a marketing department. Always glossy, the actors always beautiful, the performances measured but never really unhinged. 

Somehow I find myself missing movies that felt a little more dangerous. Not just “edgy.” I mean you could feel somebody making choices.

Sometimes the choices were wrong or scenes just wandered off somewhere weird for ten minutes. Somebody cast a face that wasn’t conventionally beautiful. Or the hero acted like an asshole. The couple didn't always ride off into the sunset together and everything was not always a happy ending.

But you knew that a person had made the thing. An artist. A storyteller trying to say something about the world. 

I’m about to start shooting a very small movie, and that idea has increasingly become the thing I care about most: I don’t want it to feel professionally anonymous.

I’d rather make some mistakes people can actually feel.

### Top 7 comments and their replies (up to depth 10)

1. You're not getting old, you're just watching the wrong movies for some reason. Your comment is like going to a beautiful part of the world and never leaving the nearest McDonald's, then complaining it's all soulless commercialism.

There are so many talented filmmakers working at the moment making beautiful movies. If you want to be a good filmmaker yourself, you need to be watching the very best of what's being made at the moment, and not acting like it doesn't exist.

I'll be more specific: you need to watch films like Blue Heron, Sentimental Value, My Father's Shadow, Hard Truths, A Real Pain and All We Imagine as Light - to name just a handful of films released in the last few years that have blown me away. There are so many more worth your time.

Edit: comment is rising, so let me please add Monster, Bird, The Ballad of Wallis Island, La Chimera and Chicken for Linda to my list!
  - Man I’m so happy to see Mike Leigh’s Hard Truths, one of the most uncomfortably human films I’ve ever seen. Nothing is flashy or anything, not much exciting happens in the film, just this scared lady going through a phase of her life, and that ending was just perfect, I was hoping it would go on longer, I was hoping for something but in typical Leigh fashion it ends right where it should and we’re left asking the questions. 

So, in the interest of making this comment not being removed, I might ask you: do you think Pansy goes to help her husband? I feel like it’s one of the more difficult decisions for her, where she’s actually needed, she needs to be the caring person, so much to say about that film- anyway, what do you think Pansy did? And that poor husband just kind of winging it through life and marriage.
  - This is definitely true, but can you not also make the argument that "mainstream" Hollywood movies have gotten worse, more soulless, and more like they're made by an algorithm?

To use use your McDonalds analogy, many people swear that McDonalds used to be decent, and only recently (last 20 years or so) has become complete shit. 

We used to have great directors make mainstream commercially oriented movies and their individuality still shined through. I don't know if that happens as often nowadays, but even when you occasionally get a great director do a Marvel or something (e.g. Chloe Zhao), you don't really see their identity. It's all subsumed by the brand.

At least that's how it feels. It could just be my bias speaking, it's not like I've examined it very deeply.
  - I mean, a lot of what you're saying is true, but you've phrased it in a manner a bit more condescending than necessary.

## 2. Sunshine's Third Act Trades Realism With Shock Value

**Score:** 4
**Body:** Like Honestly, WTF WAS THAT THIRD ACT?

Such an amazing, beautiful, psychologically profound, thought provoking, visually stunning, flawless, all-star movie with amazing special effects is marred by such rushed, lazy storytelling in the end. Unexplained moments, an abrupt genre change, it just kills the mood.

Danny Boyle left no room to disturb the viewer and went so unorthodox and unconventional, camera angles, cuts, use of colors, music, everything was so well put, until Boyle himself didn't know what else to do.

The movie's flavor was spoiled the moment blood entered the frame, and how so? In the most illogical and unexplainable way. At once I had hope that it might be a dream sequence, but after realizing it wasn't, my jaw was on the floor. I was like WTH.

I know the movie technically foreshadows (or I'm just speculating) three things to prove Pinbacker's alive:

1. The food storage scene, where the crew on Icarus 2 discusses that the food wouldn't be enough for all of Icarus 1's crew members, so some of them should've died. Hence he was the only one left alive. This part makes sense somehow.

2. The video messages from Pinbacker, especially the one on Icarus 1, which shakes to reveal Pinbacker's figure...

3. ...And the amazing garden in there

But.

Even if Pinbacker's alive, they still shouldn't have blurred the lines between surrealism and realism like this. That transition is jarring, since the movie leaves no room for the audience to even entertain something surreal in the first 60 minutes. It's raw, realistic, hard hitting, concrete, and purely scientific. That's what it achieves in the first hour. If you want to bring a Hollow Man into this, at least foreshadow it properly or prepare us for it.

And even then, Pinbacker's survival and him hiding on Icarus 2 still doesn't make any real sense. It's speculated, not seeded, not explained. Surviving seven years alone, sneaking aboard undetected during docking, hiding on a small ship with a full crew watching everything, we're just told this happened after the fact, we never know how and when did he do it.

And most importantly, there was no need for the movie to create a good guy/bad guy dynamic at all. The stakes were already far higher than needing a moral antagonist, this was the survival of mankind. So high that if a crew member decides to get scorched by the sun, or gets stranded on an abandoned ship, or even commits suicide, all of that makes sense on its own. Why then insert a glitching ghost in flesh that just kills people without properly explaining his arrival or motive? He comes so abruptly it breaks the whole film's internal logic.

I get Pinbacker's reasoning too, (speculating here btw) that he didn't want the sun to be meddled with, which is probably why he killed his crew and abandoned the mission 7 years ago. Still, that's not the way to introduce or execute that idea.

I felt betrayed, honestly. It hurts when you invest 60 minutes into a one of its kind existential sci-fi space dread movie and suddenly it turns into A Nightmare on Elm Street. It also hurts when such an amazing film, with such a brilliant cast meticulously collected like Infinity Stones, suffers through such bad execution in the end.

## 3. Between Possession (1981) and Szamanka (1996) I think Zulawsky came to see the ecstatic actress as a vampiric Shaman

**Score:** 1
**Body:** There is a ton packed into Zulawsky's remarkable, much less seen Szamanka (She-Shaman), ([this article](https://www.fangoria.com/post-possession-andrzej-zulawskis-szamanka-at-twenty-five/) does a quick job of hitting important dimensions), but the overriding sense of significance for me in this possible spiritual sequel to the unparalleled Possession is really in the ecstatic/primal female figure of the main characters. Anna vs The Italian (Isabella Adjani vs Iwona Petry). I'm not going to be reductive about it because both these films feel unfathomable, in different ways, but there is the sense that when The Italian in  Szamanka is >!eating the professorial brains in the end, inhabited as she is by a she-shaman spirit who did the same of the bog-preserved medicine man!<, not far from the culminating carnivorous scene in von Kleist's 1808 play "Penthesilea", the reversal of Possession has been completed. In Possession it is a rising superstar French actress in Adjani (filmed by her husband on set), in Szamanka it is a near first-time actress found in a cafe, if I recall. The power dynamics are incredibly different. In Possession, in terms of plot, it is "she" who leaves her husband for the otherworldly, demonic lover, in Szamanka is it the husband who leaves the wife for the same. In Possession, Anna is not feeding off of Sam Neil's character (Zulawsky's stand-in) in the least, in fact she is claustrophobically smother by him and what he represents. He instead must gradually surrender his autonomy and follow her into descent.

My intuition is telling me that 15 years on, Zulawsky who held something of a "shamanistic" concept of what acting should be - an "artificial" performance, which through that rite artifice channels something hyper real and intensely primal/human - shifted in his belief of what the actress is doing. In Possession he rides the incredible wave of Adjani's out-of-body performance, Adjani shamanistically animating the entire film with primal, "demonic" energies upon which everyone feeds, including one imagines the director himself, but in Szamanka it is that the actress who in terms of plot has >!become vampiric upon the "brains" of the (expert) director, stealing away from his knowledge!<, just as >!the bog-man was stolen from!<. Zulawsky, notably as a grudge-bearing man, it seems has come to see the actress as siphoning off from the film production itself, and certainly his own older experience as as director. As he even tried to advise Adjani, who reportedly exaggeratedly was desperate for her career and life (according to Zulawsky's possibly unreliable report): He and the film will take the heat of the backlash, but she will come out unscathed as the star. With irony perhaps, while Adjani went onto becoming more and more powerful in film, Iwona Petry went from obscurity back to relative obscurity.

His filming methods were notoriously intense, arguably abusive, but the two films together bookend the question: Who or what is feeding on whom?

I'm a little divided by Zulawsky as a man/director. He feels ill-motivated, angry and violent, but his films are just intensely transformative (perhaps due to his character flaws), and speak to capacities in cinema which others seldom reach.

Szamanka is not an easy film to find, but as more people are inspired to watch Possession with the remake coming, they may dig into finding Szamanka, a film I think which through its reversals helps open up what Possession was all about.

## 4. An Unintentional 'Trilogy of Trust' (The Odyssey, Obsession and Project Hail Mary)

**Score:** 1
**Body:** I'm fully aware this is going to sound like a bit of a stretch/painting patterns where they don't exist, but it's sort of been a brainworm I wanted to write a short essay about, regarding these three amazing films from this year. Plus, this is sort of my 'thing' I guess, gushing about media I love by relating it to other things, even if they have nothing to do with each other on the surface level.

It goes without saying too, these three movies vary wildly in genre, tone, scale, intention, just about everything. Nolan, Barker, and Lord & Miller all had very different ideas for their respective releases from this year. All three of them are absolutely spellbinding and I'd gladly give the rare 10 score to them, with them all succeeding with flying colours at their own missions. The thing is, even if it's just me, I happened to get a lot of emotional catharsis and thematic fulfillment from watching all of them in this order, while imagining them as either one overarching story, or simply with the same theme in mind.

The theme of trust, simple as it is, is handled very delicately in all three of them, and I wanted to explore how they do that, and how they all act as their own 'entries' in this 'trilogy'. Please keep in mind though, this is mostly just a bit of fun, and lowkey an excuse to just gush about the trio.

And of course, spoilers for all three films individually below, even if they've been out for months, just wanna be safe. Also, the word 'Trust' will come up a lot, I apologize in advance lol.

\-----

***Part 1 - The Odyssey: The Death of Trust***

**With the deception and ensuing sacking of Troy, Odysseus unintentionally destroys 'Zeus's Law'. More specifically, the unspoken rule of humanity's inherent trust in one another. A series of raids and atrocities first described by Penelope as 'The People from the Sea', are later revealed to be directly influenced and sparked by the rapidly spreading Trojan horse story.**

**Further shown to us by the Assault on Polyphemus, a direct follow-up offence which then incurs Poseidon's wrath, the (somewhat understandably) bitter Circe as she decries Odysseus's crew for their behaviour, the resentment of their fallen brethren in the Underworld scene, and Athena's continual disappointment in him up until his realization towards the end of the film, we see the beginning of Trust's total erosion, and how that will shape the future of humanity for eons to come.**

**Though Odysseus and Penelope sail into exile by the end, and hope for a better tomorrow, they know full well it will not be easy, and will lead to some truly dire acts. One such smaller scale one being;**

***Part 2 - Obsession: The Perversion of Trust***

**3,000 years pass. Despite being numerous eras removed from Odysseus's time, it still is a 'Time of Apparent Magic' so to speak, as the One Wish Willow behaves like something right out of Greek mythology. Yet it acts only as the mere catalyst for the continuation of this idea, of how corrupted and lost the idea of inherent trust has become, especially in intimate relationships.**

**Bear himself is the Trojan Horse of this era, the outwardly friendly, soft-spoken guy that Nikki Freeman believes she can talk to about things she doesn't feel comfortable talking about with Sarah, Ian, or any other confidants she may have in her life. She remains blissfully unaware, right up until he snaps the Willow in half, just how misplaced her faith was.**

**She eventually can't even trust him to care for her enough to help her out of what is clearly a catastrophic situation. Rather than attempt to reverse the cause or get her professional help, Bear takes full advantage of the Wish-engulfed Nikki and isolates her, leaving her in a state of total reliance, which just goes so unbelievably well.**

**The theme's continuation doesn't stop there, it's the closed off wall Bear puts between himself and Sarah despite her evident feelings and, by all accounts, being much more compatible with him (despite her own mistakes and flaws that ultimately doom Nikki as well), with Ian's stereotypical 'Jock' personality being rooted in toxic ideals that also compound the situation and prevent the openness all of them desperately needed, until it was too late.**

**By this point in the 'timeline', we reach the low-point, a snippet into just how bad both the lack of trust, and the act of causing one to trust you before pulling the rug from underneath them have become... and all of that leads nicely into;**

***Part 3 - Project Hail Mary: The Redemption of Trust***

**A few years to a couple decades after the events of Obsession, we reach the climax of this through line. With the Petrova line about to condemn everyone to starvation or hypothermia, very conditional 'Trust' is given between everyone working on the Project itself, chiefly in Dr. Ryland Grace himself... which is then betrayed and shown for what it is once Stratt forces him onto the mission against his will.**

**This, however, is the turning point for the Theme and the beginning of a revival. Despite being lost and scared out of his mind, Grace refuses to do anything less than his best, and strives to figure it all out. Upon meeting Rocky, he reengages Zeus's law in the best faith possible, despite a monolithically large language and anatomy difference, and the Eridian Rock does the same with little to no hesitation, suggesting they had no equivalent event to the Trojan Horse.**

**In their mission to rescue both of their worlds, Grace and Rocky form a bond forged in something stronger than the gods could ever feasibly imagine, something more genuine than Bear could ever hope for, and more organic than Stratt could've ever anticipated.**

**Trust itself is born again between the first Human-Eridian team, as they risk life and limb for each other in their darkest moments, with Grace eventually choosing to send all of the information home, forsaking his own ticket back to Earth purely out of love for his best friend, and sending not just the Taumoeba, but proof that Odysseus's original sin, that Bear's self-serving greed, and that Stratt's cold 'efficiency' had all been defeated, once and for all.**

\-----

...And with that, this trilogy I've magicked out of thin air comes to a close. I totally understand if this is a massive stretch for anybody, but I had a lot of fun coming up with this through line, again whether it means they share a timeline or merely this same delicate idea tackled immeasurably well in different ways, I love them all to bits. Let me know if you think there's another angle to the ideas here, or if you just wanna gush about any of the three that's awesome too :).

Thanks for reading my long-winded thing (not sure what to call this, but hey maybe I'll turn it into a video script, who knows!).
